scribeTiers.scribeName: The Cloud of His Anger (The LORD's Day of Wrath)
New Every Morning (Great Is Thy Faithfulness)

characters.name: The Weeping Widow — Jerusalem's Desolation (Lamentations 1)
characters.purpose: Personifies Jerusalem/Zion as a great city fallen to the status of a bereaved widow, weeping in the night with no comforter, her roads mourning, her adversaries now prospering — while the poem itself repeatedly concedes the judgment is deserved: 'The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment' (1:18). (Attribution: Anonymous within the text itself. Ancient tradition (reflected in the Septuagint's introductory note, not the Hebrew text) ascribes the whole book to Jeremiah the prophet, but Lamentations never names an author — treat the Jeremiah attribution as traditional, not textually asserted.)

verses.note: The city that was 'full of people' is now solitary 'as a widow,' weeping in the night with none to comfort her.
'Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow' — the poem's most quoted line of appeal to onlookers.
'The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment' — the lament's own confession that the disaster is just, not arbitrary.

funFacts: Chapter 1 is an acrostic: its 22 verses begin, in order, with the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet — a structural feature invisible in English translation.
Jerusalem/Zion is grammatically feminine throughout and is addressed and described as a specific bereaved woman, not merely 'a city' in the abstract.
characters.perkNote: Thematic passive-bonus motif: mourning over what was lost — flavor text only, no numeric mechanic specified here.

characters.name: The Cloud of His Anger — The LORD's Day of Wrath (Lamentations 2)
characters.purpose: Unlike chapter 1's focus on Zion's grief, chapter 2 names the LORD himself as the direct agent of the destruction — 'the Lord was as an enemy' (2:5) — cataloguing the ruin of sanctuary, king, and feast days, and indicting the nation's own prophets for having 'seen vain and foolish things' instead of warning the people. (Attribution: Anonymous within the text itself; see the authorship note on the Chapter 1 tier — the same hedge applies throughout the book.)

verses.note: 'How hath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger... and remembered not his footstool in the day of his anger!'
'The Lord was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel' — the chapter's central, startling reversal: God described in the language used elsewhere for Israel's foes.
'Mine eyes do fail with tears... because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city' — the poet's own grief breaks into the third-person description.

'Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee... but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment' — false prophets blamed for failing to warn of judgment (compare Jeremiah 23:16-17, a distinct passage, not identified with any individual named in Lamentations itself).

funFacts: Chapter 2 is also a 22-verse acrostic, like chapters 1, 4, and 5.
characters.perkNote: Thematic passive-bonus motif: judgment poured out — flavor text only, no numeric mechanic specified here.

characters.name: New Every Morning — "Great Is Thy Faithfulness" (Lamentations 3)
characters.purpose: The book's structural and theological center: a single sufferer, 'the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath' (3:1), descends into personal darkness under God's discipline, then turns — at the poem's midpoint — to the book's most famous affirmation of hope, 'his compassions fail not... great is thy faithfulness' (3:22-23), before returning to lament and a plea for the LORD to judge his oppressors. Marked out by the user's own guidance as a standout passage deserving its own tier, distinct from the four surrounding communal laments. (Attribution: Anonymous within the text itself; see the authorship note on the Chapter 1 tier. The identity of 'the man' in 3:1 is also not stated by the text — it may be the poet's own voice, Jerusalem/Zion personified as a man, or a representative sufferer for the whole community; Lamentations does not resolve which, and no identification should be asserted as fact.)

verses.note: 'I am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath' — opens the chapter's first-person lament.

'It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.' The book's most quoted lines, sitting at the exact center of its longest chapter.
'The LORD is good unto them that wait for him... It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.'
'I called upon thy name, O LORD, out of the low dungeon. Thou hast heard my voice' — the sufferer testifies God has already heard him, mid-lament.

funFacts: Chapter 3 is a triple acrostic — 66 verses in which each set of three consecutive verses begins with the same Hebrew letter, cycling through all 22 letters — making it both the longest chapter in the book and its most tightly structured.

The hope expressed in 3:22-23 is bracketed on both sides by continued lament within the same chapter (e.g. 3:1-20 before it, renewed complaint later in the chapter) — the book does not resolve into unbroken comfort even here.
characters.perkNote: Thematic passive-bonus motif: mercies renewed daily — flavor text only, no numeric mechanic specified here.

characters.name: The Fallen Crown — Siege and Famine (Lamentations 4)
characters.purpose: Contrasts Zion's former glory — 'the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold' (4:2) — with the horrors of the siege's famine, including compassionate mothers reduced to eating their own children (4:10), and lays blame on corrupt priests and prophets (4:13) and the capture of 'the anointed of the LORD' (4:20), closing with a taunt of coming judgment against Edom. (Attribution: Anonymous within the text itself; see the authorship note on the Chapter 1 tier.)

verses.note: 'How is the gold become dim!... The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers' — former splendor contrasted with present ruin.
'The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children: they were their meat in the destruction of the daughter of my people' — the siege's famine at its most extreme.
'For the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her.'

'The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the LORD, was taken in their pits.' Widely understood by later interpreters as referring to King Zedekiah's capture (compare 2 Kings 25:5-7, a separate passage) — but the verse itself names no individual, so this identification should be treated as a likely inference, not asserted as flat textual fact.
'Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom... the cup also shall pass through unto thee' — a taunt-oracle warning Edom that judgment will reach her too.

funFacts: Chapter 4 is another 22-verse acrostic, though its verses are shorter (two lines each) than chapters 1-2's three-line verses.
Edom (4:21-22) is a neighboring nation descended from Esau (Genesis 36), not an individual person — included here as a named group/place referenced in the text, not a character entry of its own.
characters.perkNote: Thematic passive-bonus motif: glory turned to ruin — flavor text only, no numeric mechanic specified here.

characters.name: Remember, O LORD — Prayer for Restoration (Lamentations 5)
characters.purpose: A closing communal prayer spoken in the corporate voice of 'we'/'us,' asking the LORD to 'remember' and 'behold' the nation's reproach — lost inheritance, orphaned children, enslaved elders, hunger, and violated women — and ending with a plea for restoration ('turn thou us unto thee, O LORD,' 5:21) that the book deliberately leaves unresolved rather than triumphantly answered ('but thou hast utterly rejected us; thou art very wroth against us,' 5:22). (Attribution: Anonymous within the text itself; see the authorship note on the Chapter 1 tier. Chapter 5 is spoken in first-person plural ('we'/'us') throughout, unlike the more personified/individual voice of chapters 1-3.)

verses.note: 'Remember, O LORD, what is come upon us: consider, and behold our reproach.' Opens the closing prayer.
'Our fathers have sinned, and are not; and we have borne their iniquities' — the generation praying acknowledges bearing consequences beyond their own individual acts.
'They ravished the women in Zion, and the maids in the cities of Judah' — among the atrocities catalogued in the prayer.
'Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old' — the book's climactic plea for restoration.

'But thou hast utterly rejected us; thou art very wroth against us' — the book's actual final verse; deliberately unresolved rather than a guaranteed happy ending, a notable and much-discussed feature of the book's structure.

funFacts: Chapter 5 has exactly 22 verses like chapters 1, 2, and 4, but is NOT itself an acrostic — the only one of the five poems that abandons the alphabetic structure, which many readers connect to its closing, unresolved tone.

Lamentations 5:21 is used liturgically in Jewish tradition (e.g. read at the end of Torah readings) as a closing plea for renewal, distinct from and read after verse 22 to avoid ending on the harsher note.
characters.perkNote: Thematic passive-bonus motif: pleading to be remembered — flavor text only, no numeric mechanic specified here.

genealogyLists.note: Lamentations contains no genealogies and no bulk name lists of any kind. It is entirely poetic lament, addressed corporately to 'Zion' / 'the daughter of my people' / 'we, us' — the text names no individual person anywhere in the book, not the poet, not the besieging king, not the 'anointed of the LORD' taken captive in 4:20, and not 'the man' who speaks in 3:1. This is a genuine structural feature of the book, not an omission on this pass — there is nothing to place in a genealogy or bulk-name list for this entry.

notes:
Lamentations (canonical order 25) is 5 poems of funeral lament over Jerusalem's fall to Babylon (586 BC): chapters 1, 2, 4, and 5 are 22-verse acrostics (one verse per Hebrew letter, chapter 5 breaking the acrostic pattern though keeping 22 verses); chapter 3 is a 66-verse triple acrostic and the book's structural/theological center, containing 3:22-23 ("great is thy faithfulness") per the book-specific guidance to give it its own standout tier.

METHODOLOGY DEVIATION FLAGGED: because the book is (a) entirely poetic/anonymous — it names no individual person anywhere — and (b) explicitly instructed to use theme-tiers per its 5 laments with chapter 3 standalone, all 5 scribe tiers are role:"law" (theme/content-type) rather than any role:"manager" person-type tiers. There are consequently no submanagers, no genealogy entries, and no ageEvents anywhere in this book's index — this is a deliberate, book-driven absence, not an oversight. Every scribeTiers.managerId resolves to a matching characters[] entry (5 tiers, 5 characters, one-to-one) — no dangling references.

AUTHORSHIP HEDGE (applied consistently across all 5 tiers): the book is anonymous within its own text. Tradition (via a Septuagint introductory note, not the Hebrew Masoretic text) ascribes it to Jeremiah the prophet, plausible given his eyewitness proximity to the 586 BC fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25, 2 Chronicles 36) and the book of Jeremiah's own laments (e.g. Jeremiah 8-9), but Lamentations itself never names an author. Every tier's "deliveredBy" field carries this same hedge rather than asserting Jeremiah as flat fact.

NAMING-COLLISION CHECK: not applicable — no proper personal name appears anywhere in the book of Lamentations to collide with any other biblical figure. The one plausible historical identification noted (the unnamed "anointed of the LORD" in 4:20, likely King Zedekiah per 2 Kings 25:5-7) is explicitly hedged rather than asserted, per the accuracy rules on unstated identifications.

This is a small, fully self-contained 5-tier index reflecting the book's genuine scope — not an attempt to force a Genesis-style large person/manager roster onto a book that structurally doesn't contain one.
